extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method; scientists and mathematicians interested in correct reasoning and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze and evaluate reasoning that moves from particular observations to general propositions (induction) and from those general propositions back to particulars (deduction), including multi-step 'trains of reasoning'. Emphasizes when and how to form general statements, test sufficiency of evidence, and chain inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain and declare theorem in its broadest form of generality
rubrics_metrics.description: This theorem it is extremely important to ascertain and declare, in its broadest form of generality; and thus to place before our minds, in its full extent, the whole of what our evidence must prove if it proves any thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate the general proposition that your evidence must support in as comprehensive a form as possible. A broader general statement presents a larger object to the imagination and forces closer attention to the sufficiency of the experience appealed to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use general propositions to reveal insufficiency of evidence (reductio ad impossibile)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, instead of concluding straight to the particular case, we place before ourselves an entire class of facts...there is then a considerable likelihood that if the premises are insufficient, and the general inference therefore groundless, it will comprise within it some fact or facts the reverse of which we already know to be true; and we shall thus discover the error in our generalization by a reductio ad impossibile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test an induction by asking whether the same premises would license the whole generalization; if that generalization implies something known false, the original premises are insufficient. Use potential counterexamples exposed by the general form as a diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent reasoning in syllogistic form to test validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The value, therefore, of the syllogistic form, and of the rules for using it correctly, does not consist in their being the form and the rules according to which our reasonings are necessarily, or even usually, made; but in their furnishing us with a mode in which those reasonings may always be represented, and which is admirably calculated, if they are inconclusive, to bring their inconclusiveness to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is any doubt about an argument's validity, cast it into syllogistic (induction→general proposition→deduction) form so inconsistencies or gaps become visible. The syllogism is a security for correctness, not a required psychological description of how we actually think.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate investigation into induction (establishing general rules) and deduction (applying them)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is therefore natural and indispensable to separate the process of investigation into two parts; and obtain general formulæ for determining what inferences may be drawn, before the occasion arises for drawing the inferences. The work of drawing them is then that of applying the formulæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat establishing general propositions and applying them to particulars as distinct steps: first determine what marks justify a generalization, then identify those marks in new cases. This separation aids testing and repeatable application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the roles of major and minor premises
rubrics_metrics.description: The major is an affirmation of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the conclusion rests... The minor premise always affirms a resemblance between a new case and some cases previously known; while the major premise asserts something which, having been found true of those known cases, we consider ourselves warranted in holding true of any other case resembling the former in certain given particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing an argument, identify the major (the generalization/assertion that evidence is sufficient) and the minor (the asserted resemblance or mark). Ensure each is supported by appropriate evidence or prior induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate testing the sufficiency of evidence with the original induction
rubrics_metrics.description: But I can not concede that this recognition of the sufficiency of the evidence—that is, of the correctness of the induction—is a part of the induction itself...The testing of the process is not the process itself; and, besides, may have been omitted altogether, and yet the process be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that verifying or reflecting on whether evidence was sufficient is a retrospective operation separate from the initial inductive inference. Making the verification part of the induction misunderstands the psychology of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the minor premise is not directly observable, establish it by further inductions (trains of reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trains of reasoning exist only for the sake of extending an induction founded...to other cases in which we not only can not directly observe the fact which is to be proved, but can not directly observe even the mark which is to prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build chains of inductions: establish intermediate generalizations (marks) that allow you to infer the minor premise, and iterate as needed. Example: chemical tests → identification as arsenic → inference of poisonous nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine and use distinguishing marks and marks-of-marks
rubrics_metrics.description: We determine once for all what are the distinguishing marks by which such cases may be recognized...These marks we either recognize at once, or by the aid of other marks, which by another previous induction we collected to be marks of the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly record which observable marks justify applying a generalization, and when necessary record secondary marks that indicate the primary ones. This bookkeeping allows multi-step inferences to be justified and checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure each induction in a train is grounded on appropriate sets of instances that converge in result
rubrics_metrics.description: Two separate inductions must have taken place to render this chain of inference possible; inductions founded, probably, on different sets of individual instances, but which converge in their results, so that the instance which is the subject of inquiry comes within the range of them both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-step reasoning, verify that each inductive generalization was supported by relevant observed instances and that the different inductions legitimately converge on the case under examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whenever possible, convert particular→particular arguments into induction→application form to test them
rubrics_metrics.description: When, therefore, we argue from a number of known cases to another case supposed to be analogous, it is always possible, and generally advantageous, to divert our argument into the circuitous channel of an induction from those known cases to a general proposition, and a subsequent application of that general proposition to the unknown case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an argument seems to jump from particulars to particulars, restating it as an induction followed by deduction often makes defects visible and aids in assessing warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that general propositions can harden into unexamined maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences originally made on insufficient evidence become consecrated, and, as it were, hardened into general maxims; and the mind cleaves to them from habit, after it has outgrown any liability to be misled by similar fallacious appearances if they were now for the first time presented; but having forgotten the particulars, it does not think of revising its own former decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against intellectual inertia: store and periodically re-examine the particulars and evidence underlying generalizations to avoid persisting in erroneous maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Logic (syllogism) is primarily the Logic of Consistency and an auxiliary to the Logic of Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The end aimed at by Formal Logic...is not truth, but consistency. It has been seen that this is the only direct purpose of the rules of the syllogism... The Logic of Consistency is a necessary auxiliary to the logic of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal logical rules to check consistency of inferences and applications of general propositions, but remember they do not by themselves establish empirical truth—empirical inductions do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make inductions once for all and register results for later application where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The inductions may be made once for all: a single careful interrogation of experience may suffice, and the result may be registered in the form of a general proposition, which is committed to memory or to writing, and from which afterward we have only to syllogize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When well-founded, codify generalizations so future reasoning can use them efficiently; but ensure records include basis and limits so future users can judge applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generality to expose all possible parallel cases at once
rubrics_metrics.description: But by ascending to the general proposition, we bring under our view not one parallel case only, but all possible parallel cases at once; all cases to which the same set of evidentiary considerations are applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing an inference, consider the class defined by the generalization to see whether other members are counterexamples or reveal insufficiency of premises.
